headings.title: Introduction to Body Cavities
headings.content: Body cavities are internal spaces within the human body that protect, separate, and support internal organs. These spaces keep delicate structures safe from trauma and allow for organ shape changes during activity, such as lung expansion or stomach digestion. The human torso and head are divided into two main cavities: the dorsal cavity and the ventral cavity. These two spaces are separated by physical barriers, bones, and membranes, creating an organized internal layout essential for clinical assessment and diagnostic charting.

headings.title: Dorsal Body Cavity: Cranial and Spinal Regions
headings.content:
The dorsal body cavity sits near the posterior surface of the body and houses the structures of the central nervous system. It is subdivided into two continuous regions:

- **Cranial cavity**: Formed by the skull bones, this rigid space encases, protects, and cushions the brain.
- **Spinal cavity**: Formed by the vertebrae of the spinal column, this long canal encloses and protects the spinal cord from mechanical injury.

headings.title: Ventral Body Cavity and the Diaphragm
headings.content: The ventral body cavity is the larger anterior cavity of the human body. It contains the visceral organs, which are often called viscera. A major skeletal muscle, the **diaphragm**, divides this large anterior space into two distinct sections: the superior thoracic cavity and the inferior abdominopelvic cavity. Understanding this separation helps nurses pinpoint the exact anatomical location of patient complaints during physical examinations.

headings.title: Thoracic Cavity Structures and Contents
headings.content:
Enclosed by the rib cage, the thoracic cavity occupies the upper chest. It contains vital organs responsible for respiration and circulation. Inside this space, smaller compartments exist:

- **Pleural cavities**: Two lateral spaces that each surround a lung.
- **Pericardial cavity**: A central space that encloses the heart.
- **Mediastinum**: The central tissue mass between the pleural cavities that houses the heart, trachea, esophagus, and major blood vessels.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Cavity and Quadrants
headings.content: The abdominopelvic cavity is a continuous large space stretching from the diaphragm down to the pelvis. Although continuous, clinicians often divide it into an upper abdominal portion and a lower pelvic portion. To accurately document pain or masses, healthcare providers split the area into four quadrants: **right upper quadrant (RUQ)**, **left upper quadrant (LUQ)**, **right lower quadrant (RLQ)**, and **left lower quadrant (LLQ)**. For instance, acute appendicitis typically presents with tenderness localized specifically in the right lower quadrant.

headings.title: Serous Membranes and Their Functions
headings.content: The walls of the ventral body cavities and the outer surfaces of internal organs are covered by thin, slippery double-layered membranes called **serous membranes**. The layer touching the organ is the **visceral layer**, while the outer layer lining the cavity wall is the **parietal layer**. Between these two layers lies a narrow, fluid-filled space. The serous fluid reduces friction caused by organ movement, such as the rhythmic beating of the heart or the inflation of the lungs.

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Knowledge of body cavities directly guides physical assessment and clinical documentation. When charting pain, abnormal breath sounds, or palpable masses, nurses use cavity landmarks to communicate clear findings to the medical team. Misidentifying anatomical boundaries can lead to charting errors or delayed interventions during emergencies. Recognizing how inflammation affects specific cavities, such as in peritonitis or pleurisy, ensures targeted patient care and accurate monitoring.
